extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and appellate judges (those litigating or reviewing reissue applications under 35 U.S.C. § 251)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standard and practical criteria for assessing whether reissue claims comply with the "original patent" requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 251 (i.e., whether the reissue claims are directed to the invention disclosed in the original patent). Targets analysis used by examiners, the PTAB, and appellate courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original patent requirement (35 U.S.C. § 251)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims must be directed to "the invention disclosed in the original patent." A reissue that changes the scope of the original patent must still claim the same invention as shown on the face of the original instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the original specification and claims to the reissue claims; the reissue must "fully describe[] and claim[] the very invention intended to be secured by the original patent" (U.S. Indus. Chem.). If the reissue claims cover a different invention than that disclosed originally, they fail § 251.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-of-the-instrument comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the reissue and original patents are 'for the same invention' is determined by comparing the disclosures on the face of the original and reissue instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determination turns on whether it "must appear from the face of the instrument that what is covered by the reissue was intended to have been covered and secured by the original" (U.S. Indus. Chem.). Perform a side-by-side textual and drawing comparison; do not rely on extrinsic intent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral/necessary element cannot be omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: If the original specification treats a particular element as an integral, necessary, or sole means for performing a claimed function, omitting that element in reissue claims renders those claims invalid under § 251.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for language that describes an element as the only disclosed mechanism to perform a function (e.g., the specification here discloses "a plurality of magnets" as the only structure for removably securing the grill). Omission of such an element is analogous to omission of 'water' in U.S. Industrial Chemicals or 'plurality of arbors' in Forum and will invalidate broadened reissue claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere suggestion or cursory mention is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue claim is not supported merely because the original specification 'suggested' or 'indicated' the claimed subject matter; cursory mentions do not satisfy § 251.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antares and U.S. Indus. Chem. teach that the original specification must 'explicitly and unequivocally' describe the reissue invention; a passing reference or brief suggestion of an alternative is not enough to permit broadening on reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening to undisclosed alternatives to an essential feature fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue claims that broaden a limitation to cover alternatives that were not disclosed, where that limitation appeared essential in the original disclosure, do not satisfy the original patent requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original disclosure presents a particular feature (e.g., magnets) as the means for achieving a function, reissue claims cannot generically recite the function without that feature unless the original explicitly and unequivocally disclosed the alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-role analysis (distinguish essential vs superficial features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the omitted limitation played a described functional role or was merely a superficial/configurational detail; omission may be permissible if the limitation had no functional importance in the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Peters as guidance: omissions of features that had no described functional significance (e.g., tapered shape with no functional importance) may be acceptable. Conversely, if the limitation is tied to the claimed function, omission is likely invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: No express statement of criticality required to find an element essential
rubrics_metrics.description: An element may be deemed essential even without an express statement in the specification that it is 'critical' or 'necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts infer essentiality from the overall disclosure when the specification treats the element as the only way to accomplish the invention's function (see Forum, U.S. Indus. Chem.). Do not require explicit 'criticality' language to conclude the element is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of POSITA to substitute an alternative is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a person of ordinary skill in the art could conceive of replacing the disclosed element with another mechanism to achieve the same result, that fact alone does not satisfy § 251.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forum and U.S. Indus. Chem. make clear that the mere possibility that POSITA could effect the invention without the omitted element is insufficient; the original specification itself must disclose the alternative or present the omitted feature as optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description/§112(a) is distinct from §251 original-patent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction of the written description requirement does not automatically satisfy the original patent requirement of § 251; the § 251 inquiry is an independent limit on reissue broadening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolution Eyewear's result was tied to written-description analysis; courts (e.g., Antares) caution that proving written description support is not the same as proving the reissue claims are directed to the invention disclosed in the original patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-embodiment disclosure increases risk of invalid broadening
rubrics_metrics.description: When the original patent describes only a single embodiment characterized by particular structural elements, reissue claims that broaden beyond that embodiment are likely to fail § 251.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification contains only one example and no disclosure of alternatives or optionality (as with the single-embodiment 'plurality of magnets' here), broadened reissue claims that omit that embodiment-specific element will likely be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue cannot recapture disclaimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue practice is subject to statutory limits, including the prohibition against recapturing subject matter that was disclaimed or intentionally relinquished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reissue claims do not attempt to reassert coverage that was surrendered during prosecution or in the original grant; the original patent requirement is part of those statutory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for § 251 Board decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's assessment of whether reissue claims satisfy § 251 is a question of law reviewed de novo, with underlying factual findings reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply de novo review to legal conclusions about whether the reissue claims are directed to the original invention, while treating factual findings (e.g., what the specification discloses to POSITA) under the substantial-evidence standard (Forum US, Inc. v. Flow Valve, LLC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical indicator: sole disclosed mechanism for performing a function
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical flag that reissue broadening will fail is when the original specification discloses only one mechanism to accomplish a claimed function (e.g., only magnets are disclosed to removably secure the grill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification repeatedly and definitionaly ties the function to that single mechanism (quotes: 'A flattened bottom side ... is removably securable to the plurality of magnets'), this supports a conclusion that the mechanism is essential and cannot be omitted in reissue claims.
